title: Next-generation Honda CR-V coming in 2027 - CarExpert
content: We use cookies to give you the best possible experience on the CarExpert website, to analyse our traffic and make sure that any advertising that is delivered is personalised to you. To find out more, visit our privacy policy. Honda's US dealers were reportedly shown the new CR-V and Accord this week, featuring more aggressive styling and the brand's next-gen hybrid system. Honda in the US has announced a new generation of its global best-seller, which will go on sale in the US market next year with a new platform and hybrid-only power. The announcement comes as industry journal Automotive News reports the seventh-generation Honda CR-V was shown to American dealers at a conference in Las Vegas, using the brand's new dual-motor 'Honda Hybrid' system with a next-generation Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder engine and available electric all-wheel drive. Honda says it aims to improve fuel efficiency in the CR-V hybrid by more than 10 per cent. CarExpert can help you research, compare and buy so you choose with confidence. The brand is describing the seventh-generation CR-V's platform as "all-new", with greater rigidity and a "modular architecture that enables greater parts commonality". Per the Automotive News report, American dealers attended a conference in Vegas on November 11, getting a preview of "a handful of new and updated models arriving in the next several years", with "15 next-generation hybrid models" to be launched globally through to March 2030. Among these new products were the next-generation CR-V SUV, in addition to a heavily facelifted Accord, both understood to be on track for a 2027 launch in the US. According to Automotive News, the seventh-generation CR-V retains its signature upright, boxy form with more muscular rear haunches and "ultra-thin" headlights. In the US, the CR-V will move to a hybrid-only powertrain strategy, based around the new-generation 'Honda Hybrid' system that will debut in the new Avancier that will be revealed next week. A full-width LED rear light bar is said to complete the next CR-V's exterior design, while inside high-spec models will get a massive 15.4-inch centre touchscreen, with a gear shifter positioned on the steering column. Hints at the new design could come from the Acura Hybrid SUV Prototype revealed earlier this year, which previewed a more angular and muscular design for what's believed to be the next-generation RDX, which is the premium brand's version of the CR-V – much like the Lexus NX is to the Toyota RAV4. The CR-V is an immensely important model for the Japanese brand. It's the automaker's best-selling vehicle globally, and it's a major player in the United States where it even outsold the ever-popular Ford F-150 during the first half of 2026. Honda is expecting to exceed 400,000 sales for the third consecutive year in the US. It's worth noting that there may be a staggered rollout of the new-generation CR-V given its broad global production schedule – for North America, the CR-V is built both in Indiana and Ohio in the US, plus Ontario in Canada. Also revealed at the dealer event was a refreshed Accord, which is said to hit the market (at least in the US) during the back half of 2027. According to dealer accounts reported to Automotive News, the new Accord will score a "more futuristic look" with a "sweeping hood, premium grille and slim headlights that echo the coming CR-V". The more 'upscale' design is said to be aimed at entry-level luxury buyers, which shouldn't interfere with Honda's premium Acura brand in the US given its only non-SUV model is the Integra – a premium small liftback based on the current Civic. While not confirmed, it's possible the design of the updated Accord could be based on the Honda Hybrid Sedan Prototype also shown in May, which wears some of the design elements described by Honda's American dealers as well as a fastback-like rear end. Rounding out the future product conference for Honda's North American dealers was a teaser for a reborn Element crossover, the revival of a cult hero in the US. Automotive News reports executives were shown a silhouette teaser showing a boxy side profile and rear-hinged doors just like the original. Production is reportedly due to commence in 2029, and the new Element will sit between the North American HR-V (our ZR-V) and the CR-V. Should it hit the market on schedule, it will have been an 18-year gap since the first-generation Honda Element ceased production. These new products will support Honda's growth mission in the United States, targeting 1.6 million sales by the early 2030s, up from a projected 1.37 million sales this year. The Japanese brand has also committed to a US$3 billion (A$4.41b) new plant in Ohio, scheduled to open its doors in 2029. Much of the brand's projected growth will be powered by this new factory, which is forecast to add production capacity of around 240,000 units. Last week, Honda teased a new Avancier SUV ahead of its reveal before year's end, expected to take the form of a large, three-row hybrid crossover to sit atop the CR-V in the brand's lineup in markets such as Asia and Australia, where the three-row, US-built Pilot crossover isn't sold. A teaser video shared by Honda Australia reveals crisp styling with a sharply creased shoulder line and simple, L-shaped tail-lights, as well as slim lighting elements up front. The new Honda Hybrid system with electrified all-wheel drive has also been confirmed, supported by a new platform developed with an emphasis on weight reduction and rigidity. The Avancier will plug a massive hole in Honda's Australian lineup, with the last large-segment three-row SUV offered locally being the MDX that was last sold here in 2007. The US-built Pilot has only ever been produced in left-hand drive. It will finally give the Japanese brand a proper rival to the popular Hyundai Santa Fe, Kia Sorento and Toyota Kluger, while also expanding the global presence of a nameplate that has previously been restricted to models exclusively sold in Japan and China. Following its reveal, the Avancier is understood to be scheduled to commence production in Thailand from early 2027, following which it will hit the market in countries like Japan and Australia. Honda also sources the Australian-market Accord and CR-V from Thailand currently. title: CAIR Foundation v. DeSantis (CAIR III) - | Knight First Amendment Institute
content: An Eleventh Circuit case challenging Florida’s “domestic terrorist organization” designation regime On November 12, 2026, the Knight Institute and the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) filed an amicus brief in CAIR Foundation v. DeSantis, a challenge to Florida’s “domestic terrorist organization” designation regime. On September 29, 2026, Florida officials designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR)—the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization—and its Florida chapter as “domestic terrorist organizations.” The designations effectively bar the organizations from operating in the state and severely burden the ability of Floridians to speak to and associate with them.The Institute’s amicus brief argues that Florida’s designation regime is unconstitutional because it grants state officials nearly unfettered discretion to designate organizations they disfavor and because it severely burdens the First Amendment rights of designated organizations and the Floridians who wish to engage with them. The brief explains that upholding the regime would set a dangerous precedent for other states to follow, paving the way for new campaigns of political retribution and threatening all organizations that are politically unpopular. The Institute also filed an amicus brief in a separate lawsuit filed by CAIR challenging a Florida executive order designating CAIR and CAIR-Florida as “terrorist organizations.” Status: Briefing in the Eleventh Circuit ongoing on the plaintiffs’ motion for an injunction pending appeal. title: Expanded Subchapter V Is Here to Stay: Debt Limit Raised to $7.5 Million and Sunset Provision Eliminated - Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman
content:
Capabilities By             Dania Slim,             Michael Stavros By             Dania Slim,             Michael Stavros The debt limit for subchapter V eligibility was temporarily raised to $7.5 million during the COVID-19 pandemic, but that increase expired in June 2024, leaving many companies with obligations exceeding the lower threshold with limited restructuring options. For those companies, traditional chapter 11 was often prohibitively expensive, weakening their negotiating leverage with creditors who viewed a bankruptcy filing as unlikely. The Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act restores the $7.5 million cap at a time when bankruptcy filings among small and midsize businesses have reached a 13-year high and subchapter V filings are already up 50% in 2026. With the cap now more than doubled, subchapter V filings are likely to increase further in 2027. Importantly, the eligibility cap limits debt, not assets or revenue, and businesses with total liabilities exceeding $7.5 million may still qualify. Only noncontingent, liquidated debts count toward the limit, excluding debts owed to affiliates and insiders. Contingent and unliquidated claims—including certain claims in pending litigation—do not count. The higher limit is likely to spur more creative eligibility planning as debtors explore ways to bring their qualifying debt within the cap and access the benefits of subchapter V. Subchapter V offers two principal advantages over traditional chapter 11: Effects and SignificanceAmong other lenders or investors, private equity sponsors may find subchapter V a viable restructuring path for smaller portfolio companies, given the lower cost, the ability to retain equity and the absence of competing plans. Likewise, while acquiring distressed assets in a traditional chapter 11 can carry higher costs and risk, the streamlined subchapter V process may create more opportunities for distressed acquisitions. These same advantages shift the negotiating dynamics for creditors. Companies previously ineligible for subchapter V now have an additional tool to obtain favorable terms, both in bankruptcy and in out-of-court negotiations. Unsecured creditors, in particular, ordinarily lack a committee to represent their collective interests, and debtors can confirm a plan without an accepting impaired class. Creditors should reassess their negotiating position and consider alternative strategies to strengthen their bargaining power. Alert

title: How Filmmaker Jill V. Dae Turned a 3-Day Script into a Fearless Body-Swap Thriller About Empathy - No Film School
content: Shooting on location in East L.A. as real-world ICE raids made headlines, Dae blends Freaky Friday mechanics with deeply personal cultural traditions in her timely short, DEI. Some movies wait years for the "right" moment to get made, but filmmaker Jill V. Dae felt she had a story to tell right now. So rather than waiting for someone to greenlight it, she went out and made it. She blended a Freaky Friday-style body-swap premise with the vibrant, ancestral weight of Día de los Muertos into a short called DEI. We caught up with Dae to discuss how she pulled off a guerrilla-speed production, the deeply personal family history behind her script, and why the movies you don't make are scarier than the ones you do. No Film School: What was the initial spark for DEI, and what made you feel this was a story you needed to tell? Jill V. Dae: First of all, I’m such a huge fan of NFS, not freaking out at all. It’s been my dream to talk with you guys, and the pod has gotten me through so many seasons of my life here in LA. So, hello, hi! The story for DEI was born out of the vitriolic, inhumane arrests that have been happening to our neighbors across the country these last few years. But my journey with the project really started three years ago, when I became a filmmaking teacher at the Latino Film Institute’s Youth Cinema Program in East Los Angeles, in a 99% Latino community. Getting to know the children, the parents, teachers, the whole community, and having the privilege of teaching them made it impossible for me not to use my voice to say something when all the insanity began. These clever, creative, and innocent children, along with their families, were being vilified in the media and by this administration, using names and labels to dehumanize and criminalize them. I was appalled at how so many of us have lost our humanity, our sanity, watching grown adults cheer on children being torn from their families and chalking them up to a punchline. So the characters in our film were inspired by them. This story is for them. And I wanted to inspire them, just like through my teaching, to know you are not who they say you are. And you can be anything you want to be. NFS: The film puts Bryan in Carla’s body, forcing him to experience a world very different from his own. What interested you about using this premise? D: Great question. I truly believe that if people on either side of the divide had the chance to sit down with each other for just five minutes, we'd find so much more commonality than we do. Whether it be sports, faith, family, work ethic, dreams and worries, or even a beer. Yet, people so rarely elect to come together—there's too much fear and distrust. So the idea was, what if you were forced to? Under a Freaky Friday-esque body swap? Undercover in a family you so fear? I think using a supernatural premise to force our characters to walk a mile in each other's shoes (in this case, a day) is more wishful thinking for me than anything. I wish we could make this divine power come true. (And hey, stay till the end of the film!) We should feel, head to toe, what another fellow human being is feeling before we can pass judgment, let alone vote against each other's interests. That’s empathy to me. And I’m personally a big believer in karma and karmic energy, which you could call supernatural as well. I often wonder if those who enact pain on others or cheer it on believe they are eating into their karmic debt at all, if they believe in that kind of thing. And how would you feel if you were born as the person on the other side of your vitriol in the next life? A supernatural premise helps me ask the audience to consider that, and Maeve Garay, who plays Carla, does such a fantastic job in taking the audience along her soul-hopping ride from teenager to 50-year-old-man-in-teenager. NFS: Why was Día de los Muertos the right cultural and narrative backdrop for this story? JD: Continuing on my point of connection and similarities, in my (Chinese) culture we actually have a Day of the Dead as well (Qingming Festival), and I grew up around many similar Buddhist practices (Hungry Ghost Festival, etc.). ‘Qingming’ actually means clear and bright, and it’s a festival combining grief with Spring, bringing joy and renewal rather than anything too scary or dark, just like Día de los Muertos (how it’s celebrated joyfully and colorfully). Through Lucia’s character (played by Zara Castaneda), I tried to show a sense of childlike excitement for the day rather than fear of the ghoulish, an emotion that was slowly learned for us kids who were naturally scared of tombs we had to help clean on the day. In my family, there was always a large emphasis on respecting our elders and our ancestors, and a shrine for my grandfather, similar to the Ofrenda where we place offerings and candles, was always present. Something I haven’t shared before is that in the scene where Marcos (played by Erik Rolando Rozet) speaks at the Ofrenda to the family, saying about the departed: “They couldn’t become American people on Earth, but they did become American ghosts,” was something my grandfather actually said to us right before he passed of cancer from years of handling toxic chemicals at a copper plant. In the '90s, members of my family were slowly trying to immigrate to Canada, including eventually my grandfather, who waited years for his citizenship but passed away before he got it. He said to us at the hospital, “Well, I never became a Canadian citizen, so I’ll just become a Canadian ghost.” I remember hearing it at only six, but when my dad reminded me of this later in life, it stuck with me. And 20 years later, it did jerk a few tears from my dad when he watched DEI. I think for me, I want people to zoom out, past all our Earthly time and bodies, and really examine what our choices here mean in the grand scheme of space-time. Cultural festivals rooted deeply in ancestry hold a lot of gravitas when asking people to question their choices and their consequences here. And for me, it was deeply personal. NFS: What was the biggest creative or production challenge you faced while making DEI, and how did you overcome it? JD: Coincidentally and unfortunately, on our first day of production, the ICE raids rang out across Los Angeles. As in the very same morning, the first case hit the headlines, and we got the notifications on our phones as we were rolling our scene of an ICE raid. It was terrifying and awful, especially for our majority Latino cast and crew on set. You never want dystopian art to play out in real life, let alone in real time. We had to delicately navigate that, and thank God we did it all right by having permits and security and all that, since we were filming on location in the community. Neighbors past our cordons were coming out of their houses, scared that it was actually happening on their streets. I was also terrified they could come and hurt our actors out of fear since they were in full uniform. I’m so thankful for our talented producer Amina Nada, first AD Rogelio Salinas, and production coordinator Kyra Brennan for keeping everyone safe and accounted for. This was one of the most challenging production days we’d experienced. NFS: Was there a particular scene, performance, or visual choice that turned out differently, or better, than you originally imagined? JD: Without spoiling the ending, I took a wild swing in executing it, approaching it with a less-is-more/say-less mentality. Though after hearing a few wild and at times confusing interpretations of it, perhaps saying more would have helped more people understand the true meaning of our twist ending. I didn’t go to film school (whoop whoop!), so my education has always been to create, create, create, and learn from doing, so I take every opportunity to do so! Every project is always a great lesson and exercise. Hats off to Jarod Bainbridge, our VFX artist, in helping me realize some of these wild visual choices. In terms of performances, we originally had a hard time casting Lucia, the young girl, as it was close to impossible to find someone at her age who could memorize all those lines and act with such depth as she did. We were really freaking out at one point and thought I might have to rewrite her character. And then at the 11th hour, Zara Castaneda came in, and it was like the seas parted and light shone through. She was our Lucia. Rightfully so, her performance has been recognized and nominated for a Rising Tide Award at Catalina Film Festival! NFS: What did making DEI teach you about yourself as a filmmaker, and how do you think that lesson will shape what you make next? JD: I think going for our film the way that we did—urgently, fearlessly, somewhat controversially—reignited my love for indie filmmaking. When I felt the idea spark, I wrote DEI in three days, called my producer and said, "How do you feel about going into production for this film in one month?" She said, "You’re crazy, let’s do it." We didn’t stop pre-pro for the next three weeks after that call, and we were pictures up within a month (including getting our amazing lead Lochlyn Munro on board). I’m not saying that’s a great way to go about every film, but I think it reminded me, on a grand scale, to do the project that you want to see and make as soon as you can while you have the creative drive and momentum. Make the film fearlessly; don’t wait for the perfect moment because that moment was always yesterday. And I really love the saying: the film you don’t make is scarier than the film you do make. Really let that sink in. Your unrealized ideas that die in a hard drive are way scarier than doing something imperfectly and putting it out in the world. It also reminded me to keep making daring work that pushes the envelope, even if it ruffles a few feathers. Asian women are rarely allowed space to create risqué films, and I plan to change that. We’re in pre-production for my feature directorial debut, equally daring and exciting, and I cannot wait to share it with No Film School guys soon! Let’s say, in a year? Manifestation and momentum are key!

title: Marquette’s Office of Marketing and Communication receives four Best of District V awards from CASE - Marquette Today
content: The Office of Marketing and Communication has received four Best of District V awards from the Council for Advancement and Support of Education for storytelling, environmental graphics, communication initiatives and photography. Marquette was awarded a CASE Circle of Excellence Gold Award in “Editorial Portrait Photography” over the summer, which was also recognized in District V. Additional Best of District V honors included the university’s “Value of a Marquette” campaign, a Marquette Magazine feature on how the university is transforming the built campus environment, and “Walk the Line,” a participatory art experience in partnership with the university’s Haggerty Museum of Art. “Marquette has received 11 awards from CASE during the past three years, demonstrating sustained excellence in marketing and communication,” said Lynn Griffith, chief marketing and communication officer. “This recognition reflects the hard work of the team and our partners across campus to elevate the Marquette brand on a national scale.” The four initiatives recognized with CASE Awards this year include: Seeing differently: Editorial portrait photography at Marquette UniversityCategory: Photography > Portraits Marquette’s photography strategy is designed for audiences across digital and print platforms, and the goal is to move beyond documentation to creative interpretation. Each submitted portrait was representative of OMC’s approach to present images as a complete composition to complement the story. The photographers paid deliberate attention to lighting, color, composition and framing to reinforce the subject’s story rather than distract from it. Lighting is used not simply to illuminate, but to establish mood and context. Color choices are similarly intentional, functioning as narrative tools that subtly guide tone and meaning. Together, these elements create portraits that feel cohesive and thoughtful. Value of a Marquette EducationCategory: Communications > Communications Initiatives The “Value of a Marquette Education” campaign was designed to elevate the value of higher education, specifically the distinctive impact of a Catholic, Jesuit education at Marquette, during a period of growing public skepticism toward college. OMC executed a multi-channel, storytelling-driven strategy, developing a website that highlights Marquette’s achievements, mission, student outcomes and economic impact. This content was amplified through organic storytelling across social platforms, earned media placements, targeted paid advertising, a presidential op-ed in a major daily newspaper, and an economic impact report, ensuring consistent messaging across local and national touchpoints. A cohesive visual identity and narrative framework tied together graphics, long-form stories, video and print materials. Stay Awhile: How Marquette Transformed Its Campus ExperienceCategory: Communications > Storytelling Internal surveys indicate Marquette alumni love hearing about physical changes to campus, and thanks to record-setting philanthropy over the past decade, there has been a string of stories about new and impressively renovated buildings for them to enjoy. Led by a cover feature in the fall 2025 issue of Marquette Magazine, the “Stay Awhile” package of print, web, video and social media storytelling paints a vivid portrait of transformative campus change, as guided by Marquette’s 2015 campus master plan. It reveals how a decade’s worth of strategic investments not only met the university’s needs for upgraded academic facilities, research labs and residential rooms, but also served needs for human connection as well. An emphasis on creating inviting spaces has reshaped how students and others gather, engage and experience Marquette. By incorporating words, images and map animations to share this story with audience members across a variety of platforms, “Stay Awhile” helped them understand and experience this transformation for themselves, and it achieved impressive audience engagement results in doing so. Walk the Line: A participatory art experience and an invitationCategory: Design > Environmental Graphics “Walk the Line” was a participatory art experience inviting students to engage with the ideas explored in the “Life Lines” exhibit at the Haggerty Museum of Art on Marquette’s campus. “Life Lines,” an exhibit of abstract works centered on “line” as a unifying theme, was curated by Haggerty’s Curator for Academic Engagement in collaboration with a theology professor who integrated the exhibit into his class on Jesuit contemplative practices. Inspired by the professor’s teachings, OMC collaborated with an illustrator to create a series of original line drawings that included reflective prompts. The use of brand colors connected the artwork to the university. The drawings were printed on adhesive material and applied directly to campus sidewalks. A chalk line formed a continuous path between the drawings and the museum, linking them together. Students could “walk the line” to class, encountering sidewalk art that encouraged reflection. The sidewalk drawings were supplemented by outdoor banners, posters, a visitor workbook, and a local magazine advertisement. The Council for Advancement and Support of Education is the global association for professionals in advancement—alumni relations, communications, development, marketing, and advancement services—who share the goal of championing education to transform lives and society. District Five, the Great Lakes District, encompasses Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Ohio, and Wisconsin, and includes over 400 member institutions and more than 2,500 representatives. title: Gassed Out: Honda’s Redesigned 2028 CR-V Ditches Gas-Only Power for an All-Hybrid Lineup - MotorTrend
content: The popular crossover follows the path set by its closest competitor, the Toyota RAV4. Honda hopes its $3 billion investment in its Ohio hybrid plant is about to pay off. The company certainly needs it to, as the Japan-based automaker today finally announced the 2028 Honda CR-V is on the way. This is the seventh generation of the popular crossover, and let’s get serious real quick: This car is massively important for Honda. The company has moved more than 400,000 CR-Vs annually for three years in a row, so getting the new one right is of utmost importance to the bottom line. The most important aspect is that Honda will only offer customers the 2028 CR-V in hybrid form. Highly likely not by chance, this move follows the path Toyota charted when it introduced an all-hybrid RAV4 lineup for the 2026 model year. Hybrid models already represent more than half of all CR-V sales, and about 30 percent of all Honda models sold are hybrids. In other words, the automaker is rather safely hedging its bets on this move. Honda says the new 2028 CR-V will be powered by its fifth-generation two-motor hybrid system, the successor to the powertrain used in the existing version of its compact SUV. The CR-V will again use two motors and an Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder engine. However, this time the available all-wheel-drive system has an electric motor driving the rear wheels rather than a mechanical connection as found in the soon to be old AWD CR-V Hybrid. Engine displacement and power output of the new CR-V’s Honda Hybrid system are unknown, but we figure it will at least match the existing model’s 204 hp and 247 lb-ft of torque. Honda says both the engine’s and the hybrid system’s peak efficiency ranges increase compared to before. To the point, Honda says it aimed to improve the 2028 CR-V Hybrid’s fuel economy by more than 10 percent. Today’s model yields 43/36/40 mpg city/highway/combined with FWD, and 40/34/37 mpg city/highway/combined with AWD if we look at its EPA mpg ratings. This means a 10 percent increase would bring those figures up to 47/40/44 mpg and 44/37/41, respectively. Our back-of-the-napkin math indicates the new 2028 CR-V’s fuel economy will finally be closer to the hybrid-only Toyota RAV4’s EPA-rated figures of 47/40/43 mpg (FWD) and 46/39/42 mpg (AWD). As for other changes? Despite the confirmation of the redesigned SUV’s hybrid-only powertrain, other details on the next-generation 2028 Honda CR-V remain scant. Honda confirmed the seventh-generation CR-V will be underpinned by a new platform with the aim of improving rigidity and lightness. A teaser image shows the CR-V logo adopting a new font, suggesting the compact crossover could also deliver edgier styling than we get with today’s conservative model. The paint beneath the badge appears to be a new metallic blue, presumably the seventh-generation SUV’s launch color. Honda has been more specific about its production plans for the 2028 CR-V. It will build its new Honda Hybrid system at the Honda Transmission Plant in Ohio (TMP-O) with a mix of domestically and globally sourced parts. The CR-V’s Honda Hybrid system will be built alongside powertrains destined for other compact, midsize, and larger vehicles as the company aims to ramp up production capacity by 250 percent. Meanwhile, the Anna Engine Plant in Ohio will be retooled to build Honda’s next-generation Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder engines. Honda will also continue final assembly of CR-V SUVs in the same three North American plants as before: East Liberty Auto Plant in Ohio, the Indiana Auto Plant, and Honda of Canada Mfg. in Alliston, Ontario. The 2028 Honda CR-V arrives next year with more details and pricing to come following its official debut. In terms of pricing, expect it to start at slightly more than the existing CR-V LX base model, which begins at $33,070. Honda won’t stray too far from that number, however; we logically expect it to remain close to the rival 2027 Toyota RAV4’s starting price of $33,895. title: Next-Gen 2028 Honda CR-V Follows the Toyota RAV4 as a Hybrid-Only SUV - Car and Driver
content: Honda has confirmed that the next-generation CR-V will debut a new platform and a new two-motor hybrid system. The current Honda CR-V can be had with or without a hybrid powertrain. However, when the compact SUV’s newest generation arrives sometime next year, it’ll only be available as a hybrid. Honda’s announcement comes a year after Toyota applied the same strategy with its new RAV4. And considering over half the CR-Vs Honda sells are hybrids, the move makes a lot of sense. Apart from introducing a standard hybrid powertrain, the 2028 Honda CR-V will mark the start of the bestselling nameplate’s seventh generation. It will also introduce a next-gen platform, which the automaker claims will prioritize stiffness and lightness; its modular nature will promote parts sharing too. While we’re still eagerly waiting for Honda to release more details about its next CR-V, the automaker has shared some breadcrumbs about its hybrid powertrain. See all results for new 2028 Honda CR-V for sale near 30303 The new fifth generation of Honda’s two-motor hybrid system will once again pair with an Atkinson-cycle four-cylinder gas engine. We don’t yet know how much power the combo will make, but Honda says it “will greatly increase the standard power and efficiency.” When it comes to efficiency, the next-gen hybrid system is targeting an improvement of over 10 percent compared with the outgoing version. For reference, the current CR-V hybrid makes 205 horsepower, and it’s rated at up to 38 mpg combined. We expect the 2028 Honda CR-V to be revealed sometime later this year. Honda says it’ll be the first of several hybrid models that it plans to launch by 2030. title: Tested: The V-12 Mercedes-Maybach S680 Is Too Much, Which Is Just Right - Car and Driver
content: The Maybach is a throwback rich with modern comforts, and for those with the dough, it’s a deal. Some things are meant for showing off: engagement rings, watches, fancy manicures, face tattoos. If nobody notices, what was the point of spending all that money? Other purchases are more subtle, like a well-cut jacket or a youthful neck. They make you look rich, but nobody can quite pinpoint why. The 2027 Mercedes-Maybach S680 is the first kind. There’s no modesty to the Maybach, but as a symbol of prosperity, it won’t be ignored. Maybach models are for buyers who think the S-class is nice but could make do with more. More bespoke badging, more unique colorways—and more cylinders, at least for lucky shoppers in Asia, the Middle East, and here in the United States. We get the option of a twin-turbocharged 6.0-liter V-12, a gem rarer than a diamond in these mini-mill times. Maybach also offers the S580 with a twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8, which is far more sensible, quicker, and more fuel efficient . . . but nobody should shop a Maybach with any of those descriptors in mind. The Maybach is nearly 18 feet of two-tone paint and illuminated callouts. The front grille is a waterfall of chrome flanked by lacy insets of repeated Maybach logos. The LED headlights are three-pointed stars surrounded by rose gold. Even the Maybach badges on the C-pillars glow to ensure that at no time, day or night, will anyone fail to notice what you’re driving. And people do notice. At a gas station stop, a man in a Honda called over from the opposite pump, “Hey, that’s some hard work right there.” If I had purchased the car myself, I would have felt proud to have my effort recognized. As it was, I admitted to stolen valor, but I still drove off floating on air. That wasn’t from the compliment, though; the Maybach uses a new air-spring suspension that can anticipate bumps and potholes using cloud-based data from other Mercedes cars on the same road for real-time predictive damping. With its long, 133.7-inch wheelbase and outrageously kitted-out back seat (we’ll get to that), it’s obvious that the S680 was designed with rear passengers in mind, but it’s so fun to drive that I’m tempted to take up a chauffeur job. The V-12 is as smooth as a beurre blanc and as meaty as the filet beneath it. It doesn’t move out with the instant response of a V-8 or an electric setup, but such haste is unseemly. Instead, it steps out with authority and builds up steam like a locomotive pulling a private railcar. The only stumble it makes is when the stop-start system kicks the V-12 back into action. Unlike with the V-8’s 48-volt assist, a noticeable shudder accompanies the return of the 12-pot’s combustion. Thankfully, it’s a problem easily solved by deactivating the system with a single push of a button. It’s not like you’re getting good fuel economy with this monster anyway. The S680 is a thirsty machine, with an EPA combined fuel-economy estimate of 14 mpg. Our test car was a mossy silver and white two-tone with a sage leather interior, and that’s the only thing green about it. At least you’ll get lots of compliments at every single gas station. The steering and its optional rear-axle assist makes the long car turn in a relatively small circle, and the brakes (15.4-inch ventilated and cross-drilled rotors in the front, 14.2-inch ventilated units in the back) do a heroic job of stopping all 5336 pounds. At the test track—where technical editor Dan Edmunds would not let me ride in the back during testing despite my assertion that it would be more accurate to the car’s use case—the Maybach accelerated to 60 mph in 4.5 seconds. At the world’s fanciest drag strip, it would cross the quarter-mile mark in 12.6 seconds at 118 mph. Edmunds brought it back down to zero from 70 mph in 177 feet without a hint of brake fade. Most impressive, the S680 whipped up 0.90 g of grip around the skidpad. Not bad for something my neighbor Shirley described as “bigger and nicer than my whole house.” The Maybach is not actually bigger than Shirley’s house, but she doesn’t have a leather-covered massaging recliner. The S680 has four. Our test car was equipped with the $6000 Executive Rear Seat Package Plus, among many other extras, and be forewarned that if you invite neighbors, gym buddies, or your hair stylist to check out the leather-covered footrests, Maybach-branded pillows, yacht-striped wooden console, folding lunch trays, and back-seat wine cooler with champagne-flute-specific cup holders, they might be unwilling to vacate the premises. I thought I might have to give the car back with a full crew inside. The Maybach is excessive. It’s not about providing a quiet space or restrained elegance. Every surface that isn’t covered in leather or wood is an interactive screen. The Maybach gets Benz’s theater-wide Superscreen with a 12.3-inch driver display that merges with a 14.4-inch center screen and a 12.3-inch passenger display. Everything glows, or is gold, or is both golden and glowing. In some of Mercedes’s other cars, the Superscreen feels tacky, like a Times Square billboard, but among the lights and quilted details of the Maybach, it’s just one more sparkly surface. The screen is the main control center for all the electronic luxuries, which Maybach is equally generous about providing. Driver-assistance technologies include all the usual crash-avoidance systems and multi-view cameras, plus parking assist with wheel rim protection (something you’ll want if, like our car, your example has $1300 worth of 21-inch wheels). While the assists can feel overbearing, like a too-attentive waiter hovering over your table with the crumb scraper, the cameras and sensors make parking and maneuvering this massive car much less stressful. At $291,600 as tested, the V-12 Maybach is not going to be on everyone’s shopping list, but in the elite scene of ultra-high-end taxicabs, it’s a bargain compared to offerings from marques like Rolls-Royce or Bentley.
